\chapter{Where a Clause Ends, and What Goes Inside One}
\label{ch:hi-clause-as-object}
\hlchaptermodality{69}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say where a Hindi clause ends -- on its verb -- and hang a whole second clause on a thinking verb with ki.}

Complete HI-R69-reported and say that you think the tea is good, then name the last word of each of the two halves.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kriyā ant meṁ]{The verb goes last}

\label{lesson:HI-C69-verb-last}



\begin{quote}
Say two sentences you have had since chapter two and chapter five: \textbf{\hi{मेरा} \hi{नाम} \hi{मीरा} \hi{है}}, and \textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{हिंदी} \hi{बोलता} \hi{हूँ}}. Now listen to where each one ENDS.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a rule you have been obeying for sixty-eight chapters}]
Every Hindi sentence in this book puts its \textbf{verb at the end}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{मेरा} \hi{नाम} \hi{मीरा} \hi{है}} — my name Mira \textbf{is}
  \item \textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{हिंदी} \hi{बोलता} \hi{हूँ}} — I Hindi \textbf{speak}
  \item \textbf{\hi{यह} \hi{किताब} \hi{है}} — this book \textbf{is}
\end{itemize}

You have seen this a hundred times and no lesson has ever said it out loud. It is being said now because you are about to start joining clauses, and the moment a sentence has two halves you need to know where each half stops. \textbf{The verb is the boundary marker.} In \textbf{\hi{चाय} \hi{है} \hi{लेकिन} \hi{दूध} \hi{नहीं} \hi{है}}, the first \textbf{\hi{है}} is what tells the ear the first clause has ended.

English is the odd one here, not Hindi. Hindi's order is subject, object, verb — so is Japanese's, so is Turkish's, and so is roughly half the world's. English puts the verb in the middle and makes it look normal.

The practical form of the rule: \textbf{when you build a Hindi sentence, decide the verb first and then say it last.} A learner who starts translating word by word from English will hit the verb too early, every time.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the three sentences, and stop hard on the last word of each
  \item where the first clause of the \emph{lekin} sentence ends — \textbf{at the first \hi{है}}
  \item the order Hindi uses — \textbf{subject, object, verb}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does the verb of a Hindi sentence go? (\textbf{Last}.) Why does that matter more now than it did in chapter two? (\textbf{Because a joined sentence has two halves, and the verb is what marks the end of each}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ki]{\hi{कि} (\emph{ki}) — \textquotedblleft{}that\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:HI-C69-ki}



\begin{quote}
Retrieve the two items before this one by name: \textbf{\hi{लेकिन}}, which sets two clauses against each other, and the rule that the verb comes last. Then say \textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{सोचता} \hi{हूँ}} — \emph{I think}. You have had that verb for a long time and have never once been able to say WHAT you think.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \hi{कि} opens the room the thought goes into}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{सोचता} \hi{हूँ} \hi{कि} \hi{चाय} \hi{ठीक} \hi{है}.} — \emph{maiṁ sochtā hūṁ ki chāy ṭhīk hai.} — \textbf{I think that the tea is fine.}
\end{quote}

Word for word: \emph{I think \textbf{that} tea fine is}. Everything after \textbf{\hi{कि}} is an ordinary complete Hindi sentence — \textbf{\hi{चाय} \hi{ठीक} \hi{है}} — with its verb in the ordinary last place, doing the job of an object.

That is the trick worth seeing, and it is why the last lesson came first: you do not need any new grammar to report a thought. You need one word and a sentence you could already say. \textbf{Every sentence in this book just became something you can think, know or say \emph{about}.}

\textbf{\hi{लेकिन}} joins two halves as EQUALS. \textbf{\hi{कि}} does something different: it puts one clause INSIDE the other, as the second verb's object. Hindi keeps the main clause first — \textbf{\hi{सोचता} \hi{हूँ}} comes before what is thought, never after — so the word order is the one you would say anyway.

\textbf{\hi{कि}} is not an inherited word. It is Persian \textbf{\ar{که}} (\emph{ke}), taken whole, and it pushed aside the older Sanskrit-derived form in exactly this slot. Marathi imported the same word as \textbf{\hi{की}}. Two languages, one borrowing, the same job.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{chāy ṭhīk hai} on its own
  \item \emph{maiṁ sochtā hūṁ ki chāy ṭhīk hai}
  \item what changed inside the second half when you put it after \textbf{\hi{कि}} — \textbf{nothing}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What goes after \textbf{\hi{कि}}? (\textbf{A whole ordinary sentence, verb last, unchanged}.) How is \textbf{\hi{कि}} unlike \textbf{\hi{लेकिन}}? (\textbf{\hi{लेकिन} joins two equals; \hi{कि} puts one clause inside the other}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%95\%E0\%A4\%BF}{Wiktionary: \hi{कि}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[… ki …]{Two clauses, two verbs, two ends}

\label{lesson:HI-R69-reported}



\begin{quote}
A joined Hindi sentence has two verbs in it, and each one is the last word of its own half. Say the \emph{lekin} sentence and point at both.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{maiṁ sochtā hūṁ ki chāy ṭhīk hai}
  \item the two verbs in it, in order — \emph{hūṁ}, \emph{hai}
  \item \emph{chāy aur dūdh} — and notice \textbf{aur} joins two THINGS while \textbf{\hi{कि}} joins two CLAUSES
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many verbs does a \textbf{\hi{कि}} sentence have, and where are they? (\textbf{Two — each at the end of its own half}.) Then stop.
\end{tcolorbox}
